messages.content: Tell me the story of the evening Mullá Ḥusayn first met the Báb in Shíráz — what happened that night of His declaration?

perplexity.text:
On the evening of **22 May 1844**, Mullá Ḥusayn arrived at the gate of Shíráz after searching throughout Persia for the Promised One. There he encountered a radiant young merchant wearing a green turban—Siyyid ʿAlí-Muḥammad, later known as the Báb—who greeted him warmly, as though they were old friends, and invited him to His home.[2]

Mullá Ḥusayn initially hesitated because his companions were waiting for him, but the young man assured him that God would protect them. At the house, the Báb asked whom he was seeking. Mullá Ḥusayn described the signs taught by his spiritual master, Siyyid Káẓim: the Promised One would be of the lineage of Fáṭimih, between twenty and thirty years old, of medium height, and possess divinely given knowledge rather than learning acquired from books.[1][8]

The Báb then declared that all those signs were present in Him. Mullá Ḥusayn remained cautious and presented a difficult theological treatise connected with the teachings of Siyyid Káẓim. The Báb answered its questions with extraordinary insight. He then took up a pen and, with remarkable speed, began writing a commentary on the Súrih of Joseph—the *Qayyúmu’l-Asmá’*, regarded as the first major revealed work of the Báb.[1][2]

At **two hours and eleven minutes after sunset**, Mullá Ḥusayn recognized that his long search had ended. The Báb announced that He was the Promised One and said that this very hour would one day be commemorated.[8][10] The conversation continued until dawn, when the Báb addressed him:

> “O thou who art the first to believe in Me! Verily I say, I am the Báb, the Gate of God, and thou art the Bábu’l-Báb, the gate of that Gate.”[2][8]

The Báb then instructed him not to proclaim the news immediately. Eighteen souls, He said, had to recognize Him independently and without being summoned; these became the **Letters of the Living**, the first followers of the new revelation.[2][5]

Thus, in the quiet upper room of a modest house in Shíráz, the Báb’s declaration began—not with a public announcement, but with an all-night encounter between the Báb and the first person to recognize Him.

current.text:
- 1844 (May 22, just after sunset): In the upper chamber of a modest Shíráz residence, the Báb declared His mission to Mullá Ḥusayn, who sat spellbound through the night as his Host revealed verses and prayers ([*God Passes By*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21310) [paraId=para_26](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_26&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_3h.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_3h.683), *God Passes By* [paraId=para_27](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_27&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_3i.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_3i.1318)).
- 1944: Shoghi Effendi instructed communities worldwide to mark the centenary by gathering at the exact hour and minute of the declaration—two hours and eleven minutes after sunset ([*Unfolding Destiny*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21312) [paraId=para_1318](https://oceanlibrary.com/unfolding-destiny_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_1318&selectionString=unfolding_destiny_bahai_ocean_en-bl17v.0~unfolding_destiny_bahai_ocean_en-bl17v.285), [*Messages to the Indian Subcontinent*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20888) [paraId=para_2690](https://oceanlibrary.com/messages-to-the-indian-subcontinent_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_2690&selectionString=messages_to_the_indian_subcontinent_en-bl1wm.0~messages_to_the_indian_subcontinent_en-bl1wm.977)).

What began as a quiet, nocturnal encounter in an obscure corner of Persia expanded into a worldwide observance anchoring the global Bahá’í calendar.

Source: [Messages to the Indian Subcontinent](https://oceanlibrary.com/messages-to-the-indian-subcontinent_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_2690&selectionString=messages_to_the_indian_subcontinent_en-bl1wm.0~messages_to_the_indian_subcontinent_en-bl1wm.977)

current.why: Accurately cites God Passes By and the 1944 centenary instructions, but it barely tells the story the reader asked for. It skips the meeting at the gate, the signs, the treatise, the Qayyúmu'l-Asmá' and the Báb's words, and pads with later commemoration.

perplexity.why: Tells the evening's story faithfully as Nabíl gives it: the meeting outside the gate, the companions, the signs from Siyyid Káẓim, the treatise, the revelation of the Súrih of Joseph commentary, the hour of 2:11 after sunset, the 'first to believe in Me' address and the eighteen Letters of the Living. Its weakness is sourcing: the numbered footnotes have no source list, and it never names The Dawn-Breakers or quotes Shoghi Effendi's account.

verdict.gaps: none

messages.content: What happened at the fort of Shaykh Ṭabarsí? Walk me through the course of the siege as Nabíl tells it.

perplexity.text:
Nabíl’s account presents Shaykh Ṭabarsí as a seven-month ordeal, beginning as a defensive refuge and ending in betrayal. The principal stages are these:

1. **The defenders gather at the shrine.**  
   After conflict at Bárfurúsh, Quddús and his companions withdrew to the shrine of Shaykh Ṭabarsí and fortified it. Nabíl gives their number as a little over three hundred, with Mullá Ḥusayn among their leaders.[4]

2. **The first attacks are repulsed.**  
   Local forces and then government troops repeatedly attacked the enclosure, but the defenders made sorties and scattered them. Quddús’s counterattacks forced the besiegers to retreat on several occasions.[9]

3. **Royal forces encircle the fort.**  
   Prince Mihdí-Qulí Mírzá arrived with a larger army, later reinforced by commanders including ʿAbbás-Qulí Khán and Sulaymán Khán. The besiegers constructed barricades and trenches around the fort, gradually tightening the blockade.[3]

4. **The siege becomes an artillery war.**  
   Cannon and mortar batteries were brought up, and the fort was heavily bombarded. The defenders’ position deteriorated as their ammunition and food ran low; they even had to dig a well inside the enclosure because access to water was severely restricted.[3][6]

5. **Mullá Ḥusayn’s last sortie.**  
   On 2 February 1849, Mullá Ḥusayn led about 313 companions out of the fort at night, crying “Yá Ṣáḥibu’z-Zamán!” They broke through three successive barricades and routed the troops. During the charge, however, Mullá Ḥusayn’s horse became entangled in a tent rope. A soldier’s bullet struck him in the breast; he was carried back into the fort and died soon afterward. Nabíl records that seventy-two defenders had fallen by that day.[1][3]

6. **Quddús continues the resistance.**  
   After Mullá Ḥusayn’s death, Quddús directed further sorties. In one, Mírzá Muḥammad-Báqir and eighteen companions captured an enemy artillery tower, threw down its guns, and demolished the surrounding barricades. In another attack, he led thirty-six men out, returned with an abandoned enemy banner, and lost five companions.[2]

7. **Starvation breaks the fort’s material resistance.**  
   By early April, the defenders had exhausted their grain and rice. They slaughtered and ate their remaining horses, then survived on grass, carrion, bones, skins, and leather. Nabíl portrays this suffering as the final phase of a siege that military force alone had failed to end.[10]

8. **The surrender is secured by an oath.**  
   After prolonged resistance, the prince’s forces offered safe conduct if the defenders left the fort. The guarantee was confirmed by Qurʾāns and sworn assurances. The survivors—about 220, according to the account—therefore evacuated on 9 May 1849.[4][10]

9. **The promise is immediately broken.**  
   Once the defenders had emerged, the royal troops disarmed and attacked them. Many were massacred or dispersed despite the pledged protection. Quddús was taken to Bárfurúsh and killed there, while the surviving companions were subjected to further executions and humiliation.[2][3]

Thus, in Nabíl’s telling, the fort was not conquered by a successful assault. Its defenders repeatedly defeated the besieging army, but starvation, attrition, and finally a violated Qurʾānic guarantee brought the siege to its tragic conclusion.

current.text:
The siege of the fort of Shaykh Ṭabarsí began when believers, ["mostly students and recluses, built the Fort of ̱S̱hayḵh Ṭabarsí and held out against the armies of Persia for eleven months"](https://oceanlibrary.com/memorials-of-the-faithful_abdul-baha/?paraId=fn_129) — [*Memorials of the Faithful*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20907).

Here are three lines from the sources on that episode:

* ["At the time the movement had been devastated by the crushing defeat at Shaykh Tabarsi"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kjv-gospel-of-luke) — [*Will and Testament*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/the-bab_will-and-testament).
* ["built the Fort of S̱hayḵh Ṭabarsí and held out against the armies of Persia for eleven months"](https://oceanlibrary.com/memorials-of-the-faithful_abdul-baha/?paraId=fn_129) — *Memorials of the Faithful*.
* ["We resolved to depart from Núr and lend Our assistance to its heroic defenders"](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_1779&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_1g4.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_1g4.1833) — [*The Dawn-Breakers*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21308), quoting Bahá'u'lláh.

Despite their different vantage points, these passages share a view of the fort not merely as a military engagement, but as a crucible where the early community faced overwhelming government forces at immense human cost.

perplexity.why: Gives a clear, staged walkthrough that follows Nabíl closely: the gathering at the shrine, the sorties, Prince Mihdí-Qulí Mírzá's army, the artillery and the well, Mullá Ḥusayn's last sortie and death, Mírzá Muḥammad-Báqir's raid, the starvation, the Qur'án oath and the betrayal. Most details are accurate. It does not quote Nabíl directly, its footnote markers point to no sources, and it leaves out Bahá'u'lláh's attempt to join the defenders and his arrest at Ámul. A few figures (for example the 220 survivors) are imprecise.

verdict.gaps: none

messages.content: How did the Báb's pilgrimage to Mecca unfold — what did He do at the Ka‘bih, and what message did He send to the Sherif of Mecca?

perplexity.text:
The Báb’s pilgrimage took place in late 1844. He traveled from Shiraz to Bushihr, sailed to Jeddah, and then proceeded to Mecca with Quddús. There He performed the prescribed rites of the ḥajj, observing the customary practices of the pilgrimage.[1][5]

At the Kaʿbih, after completing the rites, the Báb seized the ring of the door and proclaimed three times, in a clear voice:

> “I am that Qá’im whose advent you have been awaiting.”[1][7]

The declaration was made before the assembled pilgrims, publicly asserting His identity as the Promised One of Islam.[2]

He then composed an epistle to the Sherif of Mecca. In it, He explained the distinctive features of His mission, proclaimed the advent of His Revelation, and invited the Sherif to arise and accept His Cause. The Báb entrusted the letter, together with selections from His other writings, to Quddús for delivery.[6]

The Sherif did not respond: the message was ignored at the time, reportedly because he was preoccupied with his affairs. Later accounts state that he recognized the gravity of having disregarded the Báb’s summons, but only after the Báb’s martyrdom.[6][9]

current.text:
The Báb performed the traditional circumambulation of the Ka‘bih upon reaching Mecca, and afterward entrusted an epistle for the Sherif of the city to Quddús, calling upon him to recognize His mission. As Nabil Zarandi records in [*The Dawn-Breakers*](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_426&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_ej.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_ej.2768):

> No sooner had the Báb performed the last of the observances in connection with His pilgrimage to Mecca than He addressed an epistle to the Sherif of that holy city, wherein He set forth, in clear and unmistakable terms, the distinguishing features of His mission, and called upon him to arise and embrace His Cause.
> — [The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_426&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_ej.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_ej.2768)

perplexity.why: Covers the whole arc: the journey from Bushihr with Quddús, the threefold declaration while holding the ring of the Ka‘bih's door, the epistle to the Sherif with its contents, Quddús as bearer, and the Sherif's neglect and his later realisation after the martyrdom, as Nabíl records it. It is broadly accurate. However, the footnotes are unlinked and unnamed, so the reader can't tell which accounts are primary. It also leaves out details Nabíl gives, such as the sacrifice of the lambs.

current.why: Quotes Nabíl accurately with a link, which is good primary sourcing. But it is thin: on what happened at the Ka‘bih it gives only the circumambulation, and it says nothing of the Báb's declaration there or of how the Sherif responded.

verdict.gaps: none

messages.content: Describe the Báb's examination before the ‘ulamás of Tabríz: who questioned Him, what was He asked, and how did He answer?

perplexity.text:
The Báb was examined at the governor’s residence in Tabríz before the heir to the throne, Náṣiri’d-Dín Mírzá, and a gathering of leading clerics. The principal questioner was **Ḥájí Mullá Maḥmūd, the Niẓámu’l-ʿUlamá**, tutor to the crown prince; among the other prominent divines present were **Mullá Muḥammad-i-Mamaqānī**, **Mírzā Aḥmad the Imām-Jumʿih**, and **Mírzá ʿAlí-Aṣghar, the Shaykhu’l-Islām of Tabríz**.[1][3][5]

The Niẓámu’l-ʿUlamá asked Him, in substance:

- **Who are You, and what claim do You make?**
- **What message have You brought?**
- **What proof can You offer for Your mission?**

The Báb answered emphatically:

> “I am, I am, the Promised One!”

He explained that He was the One whose advent Muslims had invoked and awaited for a thousand years, and declared that the peoples of East and West were required to obey His word.[1][2][5]

When asked for proof, He replied that **the greatest proof of a divine Messenger is His own revealed Word**. He added that He could reveal, in two days and two nights, verses equal in number to the Qur’án.[2][5]

At the Niẓámu’l-ʿUlamá’s request, the Báb then began describing the proceedings in language resembling the Qur’án. **Mullá Muḥammad-i-Mamaqānī interrupted, criticizing what he called a grammatical error.** The Báb answered that God’s Word cannot be constrained by grammatical rules devised by human beings; rather, those rules had themselves been derived from revealed Scripture. He further pointed to similar departures from conventional grammar in the Qur’án.[1][2][3]

Some accounts also record that the clerics asked Him learned questions, including one concerning the stars and planets. The Báb replied that He had not studied astronomy or astrology, and that such knowledge flowed from Him spontaneously, like His revealed verses.[4]

current.text:
When the Báb reached Tabríz, He was brought before a government tribunal where prominent divines—including the Niẓámu’l-‘Ulamá’, Mullá Muḥammad-i-Mámáqání, Mírzá Aḥmad the Imám-Jum‘ih, and Mírzá ‘Alí-Aṣg̱har the Ṣhayḵhu’l-Islám—questioned Him concerning His claims, as recorded in [*A Traveler’s Narrative*](https://oceanlibrary.com/travelers-narrative_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_46&selectionString=abdu-l-baha-traveler-s-narrative-ocean_en_41.0~abdu-l-baha-traveler-s-narrative-ocean_en_41.765) by ‘Abdu’l-Bahá ([A Traveler’s Narrative](https://oceanlibrary.com/travelers-narrative_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_46&selectionString=abdu-l-baha-traveler-s-narrative-ocean_en_41.0~abdu-l-baha-traveler-s-narrative-ocean_en_41.765)). When asked, the Báb openly stated His claim to the station of the Mahdí, which provoked a mighty tumult among the assembled doctors ([A Traveler’s Narrative](https://oceanlibrary.com/travelers-narrative_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_46&selectionString=abdu-l-baha-traveler-s-narrative-ocean_en_41.0~abdu-l-baha-traveler-s-narrative-ocean_en_41.765)).

Here are reflections on that examination across the historical and interpretive records:

* ["When the Báb reached Tabríz they brought Him after some days before the government tribunal."](https://oceanlibrary.com/travelers-narrative_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_46&selectionString=abdu-l-baha-traveler-s-narrative-ocean_en_41.0~abdu-l-baha-traveler-s-narrative-ocean_en_41.765) — [*A Traveler’s Narrative*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20899)
* ["The avowed purpose of that convocation was to arraign the Prisoner, and deliberate on the steps to be taken for the extirpation of His so-called heresy."](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_63&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_4i.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_4i.1191) — [*God Passes By*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21310)
* "Upon His arrival, the Báb observed that every seat in that hall was occupied except one which had been reserved for the Valí-‘Ahd." ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_901&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_rq.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_rq.2396)) — [*The Dawn-Breakers*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21308)

These accounts share the central recognition that a formal ecclesiastical and governmental tribunal was convened to interrogate the Báb, yet it unexpectedly became the public stage for the bold assertion of His mission.

current.why: It names the divines correctly and draws on the right primary sources (A Traveler's Narrative, God Passes By, The Dawn-Breakers). But it barely answers the question: there is nothing on the questions put to the Báb beyond His claim to be the Mahdí, and nothing on how He answered. The bullet 'reflections' are scene-setting quotations that leave the substance out, the citations repeat, and the closing summary is padding.

perplexity.why: It answers all three parts of the question in line with Nabíl and Shoghi Effendi: who questioned Him (the Niẓámu'l-'Ulamá, Mamaqání and the others), what He was asked (His claim, His message, His proof), and how He answered. That includes His proof from revealed verses, the offer to reveal in two days and two nights verses equal to the Qur'án, and the exchange with Mamaqání over grammar. There are flaws: the footnotes [1]–[5] never say which sources they mean, the famous declaration is shortened (God Passes By has 'I am' three times, not twice), and the astronomy point is weakly sourced.

verdict.gaps: none

messages.content: What is the story of the 'Sifter of Wheat' in Iṣfahán in the Dawn-Breakers, and why is it remembered?

perplexity.text:
In *The Dawn-Breakers*, the “Sifter of Wheat” is identified in later notes as **Mullá Jaʿfar**, commonly called **Gandum-Pák-Kun**. He was a humble wheat sifter in Iṣfahán and the **first person in the city to accept the Báb’s message**. He served Mullá Ḥusayn devotedly and became an ardent supporter of the new faith.[1][2]

When he later heard about the siege of Shaykh Ṭabarsí, he immediately set out to join the Báb’s defenders, still carrying his sieve. When asked why, he said he intended to “sift” the people he met along the way—finding those willing to embrace the Cause and accompany him to martyrdom.[1]

He eventually joined the defenders and was killed at Shaykh Ṭabarsí.[3] His story is remembered because it contrasts **humble spiritual insight with the failure of Iṣfahán’s celebrated scholars**: although the city was renowned for learning and religious institutions, the Báb said that only this ordinary laborer recognized the truth and received the “robe of Divine virtue.”[1] The sieve thus became a symbol of discernment, wholehearted faith, and the principle that spiritual greatness is not determined by social rank or scholarly reputation.

current.text:
The story of the sifter of wheat in Iṣfahán tells of Mullá Muḥammad Ja‘far Gandum-Pák-Kun, the very first person in that city to accept the Faith of the Báb upon hearing the call. He served Mullá Ḥusayn with devotion, became a zealous advocate of the new revelation, and eventually joined the defenders at the Fort of Ṭabarsí, where he perished during the siege. He is remembered because his unreserved acceptance and steadfastness are praised directly in the [*Kitáb-i-Aqdas*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21307), where he is noted as one who _“donned the robe of discipleship.”_ ([The Kitáb-i-Aqdas](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-aqdas_bahaullah/?paraId=fn_183))

***

current.why: The core facts are right: Mullá Ja'far Gandum-Pák-Kun was the first believer in Iṣfahán, served Mullá Ḥusayn and died at Ṭabarsí. It correctly ties his memory to the Kitáb-i-Aqdas (¶166 and note 183). But it barely draws on The Dawn-Breakers. It leaves out the Báb's contrast in the Persian Bayán between Iṣfahán's divines and the sifter, which is the main reason he is remembered. The 'robe of discipleship' wording is put down to the Aqdas a bit loosely.

perplexity.why: This is a fuller story. It gives the central meaning: a humble labourer recognised the truth while Iṣfahán's famous divines did not, which the Báb himself pointed out. It also covers his joining Ṭabarsí and his martyrdom, and draws out what the story means. Weaknesses: the line about 'sifting' people along the road with his sieve looks embellished or unsupported, and it says the name comes from 'later notes' when Nabíl gives it directly. 'Robe of Divine virtue' may not match the source, and it misses the Aqdas reference.

verdict.gaps: B gave the Báb's own contrast between Iṣfahán's learned divines and the humble sifter, which is the reason the story is remembered. It also gave more of the Dawn-Breakers narrative: how he joined Ṭabarsí, and how the story stands as a lesson that spiritual rank does not follow learning or station. A had only the Aqdas mention.

messages.content: How was the Báb martyred in Tabríz in 1850? What happened with the first volley and Sám Khán's regiment?

perplexity.text:
The Báb was executed in Tabríz on **9 July 1850**. He and His companion, **Mírzá Muḥammad-‘Alí—known as Anís**, were suspended by ropes from a nail in the wall of the barracks square. About **750 soldiers** of the Armenian Christian regiment of Urúmíyyih, commanded by **Sám Khán**, fired in three successive volleys.[2][5]

When the smoke cleared, Anís was still alive and unharmed, while the Báb had disappeared from the wall. The bullets had severed the ropes without injuring either man; the Báb was then found back in the room where He had been held, completing a conversation with His secretary.[3][5]

Sám Khán was deeply shaken and refused to fire again or allow his regiment to participate further. He withdrew his men, reportedly declaring that he would not undertake an act that might harm the Báb, even at the cost of his own life.[3][8] A second regiment, commanded by **Áqá Ján Khán-i-Khamsih**, was brought in. The Báb and Anís were suspended again, and the subsequent volley killed them; their bodies were severely shattered.[4][5]

current.text:
I didn't find a passage detailing the exact events of the first volley and Sám Khán's regiment in this search, as the texts I can search mention the handover to Sám Khán and the general setting of the martyrdom in Tabríz, but do not describe the regiment's initial volley.

If you would like to explore the specific details of the execution further, you might search using terms like "Sám Khán" alongside the martyrdom.

current.why: Gives no information about events that are well documented in Nabíl and God Passes By. It declines to answer and only suggests the reader search for themselves.

perplexity.why: An accurate narrative that matches Nabíl and Shoghi Effendi: the date, Anís, the 750 Armenian soldiers firing in three files, the ropes severed, the Báb found finishing His talk with His secretary, Sám Khán withdrawing, and Áqá Ján Khán-i-Khamsih's regiment carrying out the second execution. It leaves out Sám Khán's earlier plea to the Báb and the Báb's reply, the Báb's warning to the farrásh-báshí, His last words to the crowd, and the whirlwind of dust. It also cites by numbers instead of naming the primary sources.

verdict.gaps: none

messages.content: What happened to Bahá'u'lláh at Ámul after He tried to reach Shaykh Ṭabarsí — why was He beaten there?

perplexity.text:
After setting out from Núr with companions to aid the besieged Bábís at Shaykh Ṭabarsí, Bahá’u’lláh was arrested about nine miles from the fort and taken to Ámul.[1][2]

At Ámul, the local clergy stirred up the population against the captives, portraying them as enemies of Islam and demanding severe punishment. The acting governor, fearing the mob and the clerics, ordered the prisoners to be bastinadoed—beaten on the soles of their feet.[3][4]

Bahá’u’lláh intervened to save His companions, declaring that they were innocent and offering Himself to receive the punishment in their place. He was therefore beaten alone, with rods until His feet bled, and was then subjected to further abuse from the crowd, including stones and insults.[2][6] He was beaten not because He had committed a specific crime, but as a political and religious concession intended to appease the hostile clergy and mob.

current.text:
Bahá’u’lláh’s journey to join the defenders at the Fort of Ṭabarsí was intercepted at Níyálá by Mírzá Taqí, the Governor of Ámul, who surrounded the village by night and brought Him back to Ámul with a small escort of riders. There, local authorities and clergy delivered Him into the hands of assembled divines who subjected Him to severe abuse and a bastinado.

The authorized interpretation by 'Abdu'l-Bahá notes that "The Blessed Beauty was confined to prison in the town of Ámul, and, as the ‘ulamá gathered together in the mosque, He was delivered into their hands. Those iniquitous divines then rose up against Him with injustice and tyranny." ([Light of the World](https://oceanlibrary.com/light-of-the-world_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_115&selectionString=light_of_the_world_baha_i_ocean_en-bl61.0~light_of_the_world_baha_i_ocean_en-bl61.556)) — [*Light of the World*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20906).

current.why: The quotation from 'Abdu'l-Bahá is a good primary source, and the interception and handover to the divines are right. But it never answers the 'why': it leaves out the clergy's agitation, Bahá'u'lláh taking the punishment in His companions' place, and the governor's role. Calling a historical passage an 'authorized interpretation' is a muddle, and the citation is padded with duplicate links.

perplexity.why: It gives the fuller story Nabíl tells: the arrest near the fort, the clergy stirring up the people, the bastinado ordered to appease them, Bahá'u'lláh offering Himself in His companions' place, and the motive behind it. Its weaknesses: footnotes with no named sources, no direct quotation from Nabíl or God Passes By, and possibly embellished details such as the stoning. It also leaves out the governor's later protection of Him.

verdict.gaps: none

messages.content: Who was Quddús, and what was his role at Shaykh Ṭabarsí?

perplexity.text:
Quddús was the title of **Mullá Muḥammad-ʿAlí of Bárfurúsh**, a prominent early follower of the Báb and one of the **Letters of the Living**. The Báb chose him as His sole companion on the pilgrimage to Mecca and Medina and regarded him as one of His foremost disciples.[1][3]

At **Shaykh Ṭabarsí**, Quddús joined the Bábí defenders after being released from confinement in Sárí. He became their principal spiritual leader after Mullá Ḥusayn’s death, while others directed the fort’s military operations; thus, he provided religious authority, guidance, and moral leadership to the besieged community.[2][5][8] Following the fort’s surrender, Quddús was taken to Bárfurúsh and killed on May 16, 1849.[1][2]

current.text:
Quddús was one of the Letters of the Living—an early leader of the Bábí movement—who perished alongside over three hundred believers during the crushing defeat and massacre at the Fort of Shaykh Ṭabarsí.

The sources record that he "hastened away to the Fort of Ṭabarsí" ([Memorials of the Faithful](https://oceanlibrary.com/memorials-of-the-faithful_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_712&selectionString=abdu-l-baha-memorials-of-the-faithful_en_og.0~abdu-l-baha-memorials-of-the-faithful_en_og.430)) ([*Memorials of the Faithful*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20907)), where he displayed remarkable "knowledge and sagacity," his companions ultimately recognizing his profound authority and resourcefulness ([*The Dawn-Breakers*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21308)).

> "the massacre of over 300 active believers amongst them prominent leaders and Letters of Living: Quddus and Mulla Husayn." - [*Will and Testament*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/the-bab_will-and-testament)

current.why: Very thin. It never gives his name, his place among the Letters of the Living or the pilgrimage with the Báb. It says he 'perished' in the massacre, but he was actually executed later in Bárfurúsh. The quotations are misused: the Memorials line probably describes a different believer, and the 'Will and Testament' passage looks like an editor's note, not the Báb's own words.

perplexity.why: The core facts are right: his name, his rank as a Letter of the Living, his role as the Báb's only companion to Mecca, his release from Sárí and his death in Bárfurúsh in May 1849. But it misstates his role at the fort. Nabíl shows Mullá Ḥusayn deferring to Quddús as leader from the moment he arrived, not only after Mullá Ḥusayn's death. The numbered citations point to no sources, and it uses no primary accounts such as Nabíl or God Passes By.

verdict.gaps: B gave his name, his Bárfurúsh origin, the Mecca pilgrimage, his release from Sárí and the date of his martyrdom. A had none of this.
authority_errors: current: misattributes an editorial gloss to the Báb's Will and Testament

messages.content: Who was Siyyid Káẕim-i-Rashtí, and what did he tell his disciples before his death about the Promised One?

perplexity.text:
Siyyid Káẓim-i-Rashtí (1793–1843) was the successor of Shaykh Aḥmad-i-Aḥsá’í and leader of the Shaykhí movement. He taught that the Promised One—the Qa’im or Mahdi—was already living on earth and would soon appear.[1][2]

Before his death, he urged his disciples to leave their homes, detach themselves from worldly concerns, scatter far and wide, and search for the Promised One rather than wait for him to come to them.[2][4] He described the Promised One as:

- Descended from the Prophet Muḥammad and the family of Fāṭimah
- Of noble and pure lineage
- Young—more than 20 but less than 30
- Possessed of innate knowledge
- Of medium height
- Free from bodily defects and not a smoker[1][6]

He reportedly added that he himself would not live to see the Promised One’s appearance, but that his disciples would find Him in their own lifetime.[7]

current.text:
Siyyid Káẓim-i-Rashtí was the disciple and successor of Shaykh Aḥmad-i-Aḥsá’í, dedicating his life to teaching the inner meanings of the Qur'án and preparing seekers for an imminent revelation. As his life drew to a close, he urged his followers to search for the Promised One, declaring that the dawn of the new Advent was at hand.

Shoghi Effendi records in [*God Passes By*](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_208&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_8j.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_8j.695):

> “Verily, I say, after the Qá’im the Qayyúm will be made manifest. For when the star of the former has set the sun of the beauty of Ḥu..."
> — [God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_208&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_8j.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_8j.695)

Similarly,  ‘Abdu’l-Bahá notes in [*Memorials of the Faithful*](https://oceanlibrary.com/memorials-of-the-faithful_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_690&selectionString=abdu-l-baha-memorials-of-the-faithful_en_nu.0~abdu-l-baha-memorials-of-the-faithful_en_nu.1172) that he repeatedly told his disciples:

> Ṭáhirih had caught fire. She set out for Karbilá, hoping to meet Siyyid Káẓim, but she arrived too late: ten days before she reached that city, he passed away. Not long before his death the Siyyid had shared with his disciples the good news that the promised Advent was at hand. “Go forth,” he repeatedly told them, “and seek out your Lord.” Thus the most distinguished of his followers gathered for retirement and prayer, for fasts and vigils, in the Masjid-i-Kúfih, while some awaited the Advent in …
> — [Memorials of the Faithful](https://oceanlibrary.com/memorials-of-the-faithful_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_690&selectionString=abdu-l-baha-memorials-of-the-faithful_en_nu.0~abdu-l-baha-memorials-of-the-faithful_en_nu.1172)

current.why: Uses the right primary sources: Shoghi Effendi's God Passes By (the Qá'im/Qayyúm saying, though cut off mid-sentence) and 'Abdu'l-Bahá's Memorials ('Go forth and seek out your Lord'). It is thin on biography and leaves out the signs of the Promised One that Nabíl records, which are the heart of what the reader is asking for.

perplexity.why: More informative. It gives accurate dates, his Shaykhí role, his teaching that the Promised One was already living, and the signs (lineage, age 20–30, innate knowledge, medium height, no smoking, no bodily defect) along with his saying he would not live to see the appearance. All of this matches Nabíl's account, but the answer never names Nabíl or quotes him, and its footnote numbers point to no sources.

verdict.gaps: B gave the specific signs of the Promised One from Nabíl's Dawn-Breakers (descent from Fáṭimih, age between 20 and 30, innate knowledge, medium height, abstaining from smoking, no bodily defect). It also gave his dates and his statement that he would not live to see the Advent. A lacked all of this.

messages.content: Who was Manúchihr Khán, the Mu‘tamidu'd-Dawlih, and how did he treat the Báb in Iṣfahán?

perplexity.text:
Manúchihr Khán Mu‘tamidu’d-Dawlih was the Georgian-born, Christian-born eunuch who served as governor-general of Iṣfahán under Muḥammad Shāh Qājār. Though regarded as a forceful and capable administrator, he became deeply impressed by the Báb and, according to Bahá’í accounts, accepted His message.[3][5][8]

When the Báb approached Iṣfahán in 1846, He wrote to Manúchihr Khán requesting shelter. The governor arranged for the Báb to be received respectfully in the home of Mírzá Muḥammad, the Imám-Jum‘ih, where He stayed for about forty days.[5][6][10] Manúchihr Khán then visited Him, convened a gathering of prominent divines, and invited the Báb to demonstrate the truth of Islam’s prophetic mission; the Báb’s eloquence reportedly heightened the governor’s admiration.[5]

When opposition from the clerics intensified and the Báb was ordered toward Tihrán, Manúchihr Khán protected Him rather than allowing Him to fall into hostile hands. He secretly transferred the Báb to his own residence, the Imārat-i-Khurshīd, where the Báb remained for roughly four months under the governor’s protection.[5][8] Bahá’í sources further state that Manúchihr Khán offered the Báb his wealth and military resources, and that he repented of the oppressive origins of his fortune.[4][6] His death in early 1847 ended this period of protection, after which the Báb was exposed again to official and clerical hostility.[1][4]

current.text:
Manúchihr Khán, the Mu‘tamidu'd-Dawlih, was the governor of Iṣfahán who extended protection and deep respect to the Báb upon His arrival in the province, offering Him lodging and later housing Him in his own private residence for safety.

The sources record that he conceived and carried out a design for the Báb's protection, lavishing honors upon Him in the privacy of his home until his passing.

perplexity.why: Gives a full and mostly accurate account that matches Nabíl and God Passes By: a Georgian eunuch born Christian; the Báb's letter asking for shelter; forty days at the Imám-Jum'ih's house; the gathering of divines; the pretended departure for Tihrán; four months in the 'Imárat-i-Khurshíd; the offer of his wealth and army; and his death in 1847. Weaknesses: it doesn't name or quote Nabíl or Shoghi Effendi (the bracketed numbers point to nothing identifiable). It gives the Imám-Jum'ih's name loosely as 'Mírzá Muḥammad'. It leaves out the treatise on the specific prophethood of Muḥammad, the Báb's foretelling of the governor's death, and Gurgín Khán's betrayal afterwards.

current.why: Accurate but very thin. It doesn't say who he was beyond being governor, gives no dates, and leaves out the Imám-Jum'ih, the meeting with the clergy, the 'Imárat-i-Khurshíd and what followed. It refers to 'the sources' without naming any.

verdict.gaps: Neither answer quotes Nabíl's Dawn-Breakers or God Passes By directly. Both leave out the Báb's treatise on the specific prophethood of Muḥammad, written at the governor's request; the Báb's foretelling of his death; and how Gurgín Khán sent the Báb away after he died.

messages.content: Who was Vaḥíd (Siyyid Yaḥyáy-i-Dárábí), how did he become a believer, and what happened to him at Nayríz?

perplexity.text:
Vaḥíd—Siyyid Yaḥyáy-i-Dárábí (c. 1811–1850)—was a distinguished Persian Shíʿí scholar and theologian. The Báb gave him the title **Vaḥíd**, meaning “Unique” or “Peerless,” and he became one of the foremost Bábí leaders and teachers.[3][5]

In 1845–46, the Sháh sent him to investigate the Báb’s claims. Vaḥíd met the Báb three times in Shiraz. As a private test, he resolved that, during the third interview, he would silently ask the Báb to write a commentary on the Qur’anic Súrih al-Kawthar. Without being told of this request, the Báb produced the commentary in a manner that convinced Vaḥíd of His divine mission. Vaḥíd returned not as an investigator but as a committed believer and subsequently devoted himself to teaching the Báb’s message.[4][5]

At Nayríz in 1850, Vaḥíd publicly proclaimed the Báb’s religion and gathered a substantial group of followers. Hostilities with the local governor led him and his companions to withdraw to the fort of Khájih, where they resisted government forces.[2][10]

A promise was eventually made that Vaḥíd’s followers would be spared and that he would be treated honorably if he surrendered. The promise was broken: the defenders were massacred, and Vaḥíd was captured. He was bound to a horse and dragged through the streets of Nayríz until he died; his martyrdom occurred on June 6, 1850.[2][5]

current.text:
Siyyid Yaḥyáy-i-Dárábí, titled Vaḥíd, was a renowned scholar who was sent by the Shah to investigate the Báb, met Him in Shíráz, and became a devoted follower after witnessing His profound knowledge and spiritual power.

Here are words from the sources on his standing and sacrifice:

- ["the number of the name of God"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/the-bab_the-seven-proofs-dalail-i-sabih#p679) — [*The Seven Proofs*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/the-bab_the-seven-proofs-dalail-i-sabih) (quoting Nicolas's note on his title)
- ["In truth the testimony of God has come and the countenance of truth is unveiled."](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/bahaullah_tablet-of-patience-lawh-i-sabr-or-lawh-i-ayyub#p42) — [*Tablet of Patience*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/bahaullah_tablet-of-patience-lawh-i-sabr-or-lawh-i-ayyub)
- ["arose to serve His Cause and quaffed his fill of the draught of certitude"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/ahang-rabbani_the-babis-of-nayriz-history-and-documents-2#p1973) — quoted in [*The Bábís of Nayriz: History and Documents*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/ahang-rabbani_the-babis-of-nayriz-history-and-documents-2) by Ahang Rabbani

When Vaḥíd arrived in Nayríz, his eloquent defense of the Faith drew large crowds and inspired profound devotion among the people, as described in [*The Súrih of Patience*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/bahaullah_surah-of-patience) (*[Súrih of Patience (Súrat as-Sabr)](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/bahaullah_surih-of-patience-surat-as-sabr#p75)*). This gathering provoked fierce opposition from local authorities, culminating in a violent siege and tragic tribulations where Vaḥíd and his companions ultimately sacrificed their lives for the Cause.

Across these accounts, the authors unite in remembering Vaḥíd as a luminous scholar whose steadfast loyalty and ultimate martyrdom crowned his transformation from investigator to defender.

current.why: Says almost nothing concrete. It skips the Kawthar test, the three interviews, the fort of Khájih, the broken oath and how Vaḥíd died. Its quotations are short fragments only loosely tied to the question, it relies on Rabbani and Nicolas rather than Nabíl, and its closing summary is padding.

perplexity.why: An accurate, well-ordered account. It covers the title, the Sháh's mission, the three interviews and the silent request for a commentary on the Kawthar, the Nayríz uprising, the fort of Khájih, the broken promise and his death by being dragged through the streets. However, it gives the date of martyrdom as 6 June; Nabíl gives 29 June 1850. Its numbered citations point to nothing, and it quotes no primary text (Nabíl, or Bahá'u'lláh's Tablet commemorating Vaḥíd).

verdict.gaps: none
authority_errors: current: leans on a secondary scholar (Rabbani's 'The Bábís of Nayriz') and Nicolas's note, not on primary accounts such as Nabíl's narrative

messages.content: Who was Ḥujjat of Zanján and what happened in the Zanján upheaval?

perplexity.text:
Ḥujjat of Zanján was **Mullá Muḥammad-ʿAlí al-Zanjānī**, a prominent Islamic scholar and religious authority in Zanján, northwestern Persia. After accepting the Báb’s message, the Báb conferred on him the title **Ḥujjat**, meaning “the Proof.” He became the leading Bábí figure in Zanján and attracted a large following.[3][4]

## The Zanján upheaval

The upheaval began in **May 1850**, when tensions between the Bábís, the local clergy, and the Qajar governor erupted into armed conflict. Ḥujjat and roughly 2,000 Bábí fighters, together with their families, withdrew to the fort and quarter of **ʿAlí-Mardán Khán** and resisted a much larger royal army.[1]

The siege lasted approximately **seven to nine months**, involving repeated assaults, bombardment, famine, and severe deprivation. At its height, the fortified area sheltered as many as 3,000 people, including women and children.[2][6] Ḥujjat was wounded in the right arm during the bombardment and died in prayer in early January 1851.[4][9]

After his death, resistance weakened. The remaining Bábís were eventually induced to surrender through promises, oaths on the Qur’an, and negotiated agreements. The Qajar forces then violated the terms and massacred many of the survivors; fewer than 100 fighters remained to face execution, while Bahá’í sources give the total Bábí deaths as at least 1,800.[1][6] The Zanján upheaval consequently became one of the most prolonged and destructive confrontations between the early Bábí community and the Qajar state.[1][6]

current.text:
Ḥujjat of Zanján was Mullá Muḥammad-‘Alíy-i-Zanjání, an eminent cleric and one of the most formidable champions of the early Bábí movement, and the Zanján upheaval was a devastating and prolonged military siege directed against him and his companions by royal forces.

As Shoghi Effendi describes the conflict in [*God Passes By*](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_110&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_5t.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_5t.1359):

> ["Unprecedented in both its duration and in the number of those who were swept away by its fury, this violent tempest that broke out in the west of Persia, and in which Mullá Muḥammad-‘Alíy-i-Zanjání, surnamed Ḥujjat, one of the ablest and most formidable champions of the Faith, together with no less"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_110&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_5t.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_5t.1359) — [*God Passes By*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21310)

current.why: It rightly turns to Shoghi Effendi's God Passes By as the primary source. But it quotes a single sentence that is cut off mid-clause and gives no account of the siege at all: no dates, no fort of ʿAlí-Mardán Khán, no death of Ḥujjat, no betrayal or massacre. That leaves the question largely unanswered.

perplexity.why: It tells the whole story accurately: the title Ḥujjat conferred by the Báb, the outbreak in May 1850, the fort of ʿAlí-Mardán Khán, about 3,000 people besieged, Ḥujjat's arm wound and death, the false oaths on the Qur'an, the massacre, and at least 1,800 dead. However, its numbered citations point to no named source. It also never quotes God Passes By or Nabíl's narrative, the primary accounts that should anchor a historical answer.

verdict.gaps: The best answer (B) gave the actual course of events: the start in May 1850, the defence of the fort of ʿAlí-Mardán Khán, the numbers besieged, Ḥujjat's wound and death, the treacherous surrender on oaths and the massacre of 1,800 or more. The other answer offered only a truncated one-sentence quotation.

messages.content: Who was Mullá Ṣádiq-i-Khurásání and what was done to him in Shíráz after he changed the call to prayer?

perplexity.text:
Mullá Ṣádiq-i-Khurásání—also known as **Mullá Ṣádiq-i-Muqaddas** and later titled **Ismu’lláhu’l-Aṣdaq**—was a Khurásání Muslim cleric who became one of the earliest followers of the Báb and a prominent early Bábí teacher.[1][3]

After receiving instructions from the Báb, he altered the **adhán** (Muslim call to prayer) in Shíráz by adding words affirming the Báb’s revelation. When he recited the amended call publicly, the city was thrown into turmoil and the governor of Fárs, Ḥusayn Khán, ordered his arrest.[1][7]

He was subjected to severe public punishment:

- He was scourged—accounts give **more than 900 strokes**, or traditionally 1,000 lashes.[1][4]
- His beard was burned or torn out.
- His nose was pierced and a halter was passed through it.
- He was paraded through the streets and bazaars of Shíráz.
- He was then expelled from the city.[1][6]

He endured the flogging with remarkable composure; one account says that after the first several strokes he became largely insensitive to the pain.[7] He and Quddús are remembered as among the first people persecuted in Persia for the Bábí Faith.[7]

current.text:
Mullá Ṣádiq-i-Khurásání was a renowned scholar, a disciple of Siyyid Káẓim, and a trusted companion of Mullá Ḥusayn who became known for his purity of life and saintliness. When the governor of Fárs was induced by local clergy to persecute the Báb's missionaries, Mullá Ṣádiq was subjected to a brutal public scourging in Shíráz alongside others after a disturbance involving the call to prayer.

As recorded by an eye-witness, 
> ["I was present when Mullá Ṣádiq was being scourged. I watched his persecutors each in turn apply the lash to his bleeding shoulders, and continue the strokes until he became exhausted."](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_445&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_f2.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_f2.1312) [*The Dawn-Breakers*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21308)

current.why: It quotes a real eyewitness passage from Nabíl's Dawn-Breakers, which is the right primary source. But it never says what the change to the call to prayer was or that the Báb ordered it. It leaves out the beard-burning, the nose-piercing and halter, the parading through the streets and the expulsion, and it describes the cause only as a vague 'disturbance'.

perplexity.why: It gives his titles (Muqaddas, Ismu'lláhu'l-Aṣdaq), explains the Báb's instruction and the amended adhán, and names Ḥusayn Khán. It lists the punishments accurately (the 900+ strokes, burned beard, pierced nose with halter, parading, expulsion), and Mullá Ṣádiq's own testimony about growing numb to the pain is also in Nabíl. It also notes, as Shoghi Effendi does, that he and Quddús were among the first persecuted in Persia. Weaknesses: the numbered citations point to no named source, there are no direct quotations from Nabíl or Shoghi Effendi, and Mullá 'Alí-Akbar-i-Ardistání is left out.

verdict.gaps: B gave the full story where A did not: the Báb's instruction to change the adhán, the name of Governor Ḥusayn Khán, the full list of punishments (more than 900 strokes, burned beard, pierced nose and halter, parading, expulsion), his titles, and his place among the first persecuted on Persian soil.

messages.content: Who was Ḥájí Mírzá Áqásí, and why did he fear and oppose the Báb?

perplexity.text:
Ḥájí Mírzá Áqásí (c. 1783–1849), born ʿAbbás Iravání, was the **grand vizier of Persia under Muḥammad Sháh Qájár** from 1835 to 1848. He exercised extraordinary influence over the shah, partly as his former tutor and spiritual adviser.[1][5]

He feared the Báb primarily because the Báb threatened his personal power:

- **A rival for the shah’s confidence:** The Báb’s growing reputation and spiritual authority could cause Muḥammad Sháh to rely on Him instead of Áqásí.[1][5]
- **The prospect of a personal meeting:** Áqásí blocked a meeting between the Báb and the shah because he feared it could lead to his loss of influence and eventual downfall.[4][7]
- **The Báb’s possible healing of the shah:** The Báb reportedly offered to cure Muḥammad Sháh’s illness. Áqásí feared that, if successful, the shah would become even more devoted to the Báb and withdraw his favor from the prime minister.[2][4]
- **Political and religious upheaval:** The rapid spread of the Báb’s message, including among influential figures, suggested to Áqásí that the movement might destabilize the Qájár state—especially amid the shah’s illness and existing rebellions.[1]

Áqásí therefore encouraged clerical opposition, prevented the Báb from reaching Tehran, and arranged His confinement first at Máh-Kú and later at Chihríq in Azerbaijan.[2][5] His opposition was thus driven by a combination of **self-preservation, fear of losing royal influence, and anxiety that the Bábí movement might threaten the monarchy and established religious order**.[1][7]

current.text:
Ḥájí Mírzá Áqásí served as the Grand Vazír to Muḥammad Sháh, holding immense political influence before falling into disgrace and poverty as described in [*Bahá’í Faith, The: 1844-1950: Information Statistical and Comparative*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/shoghi-effendi_bahai-faith-the-1844-1950-information-statistical-and-comparative). He opposed the Báb out of political preservation and fear.

- ["The overbearing and crafty Ḥájí Mírzá Áqásí, fearful lest the sway of the Báb encompass his sovereign and thus seal his own doom"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_50&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_45.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_45.3355) — [*God Passes By*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21310)
- ["Fearing that the growing popularity of the Báb might move Muḥammad Sháh to grant Him a personal audience, Ḥájí Mírzá Áqásí, the Prime Minister, set out to poison the minds of the ʿulamā of Isfahán."](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/mohammad-norozi_haji-mirza-aqasi-a-portrait-of-a-tyrannical-and-ignorant-prime-minister-with-a-2#p8) — *Hájí Mírzá Áqásí: A Portrait of a Tyrannical and Ignorant Prime Minister With a Translation of His Letter Addressed to the ‘Ulamá—the Learned Divines—of Isfahán*
- ["Áqásí echoes the invective of the clergy, portraying the Báb as both misguided and misleading, and insisting that His punishment was essential for the preservation of religion and the security of the state."](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/mohammad-norozi_haji-mirza-aqasi-a-portrait-of-a-tyrannical-and-ignorant-prime-minister-with-a-2#p9) — *Hájí Mírzá Áqásí: A Portrait of a Tyrannical and Ignorant Prime Minister With a Translation of His Letter Addressed to the ‘Ulamá—the Learned Divines—of Isfahán*

These sources share the view that Áqásí's hostility stemmed from a desperate desire to protect his own political survival and power by turning the monarch and clergy against the Báb's growing influence.

current.why: Quotes Shoghi Effendi's God Passes By directly on Áqásí's fear that the Báb's influence would reach the Shah. That is the right primary source, and the scholarly portrait by Norozi is clearly labelled as such. However, the answer is thin. It leaves out who Áqásí was (his role as the Shah's tutor and Sufi guide, his dates) and the concrete results of his opposition (stopping the Báb from reaching Tehran, the imprisonments at Máh-Kú and Chihríq).

perplexity.why: Informative and well organised. It covers the right biographical facts, his hold over the Shah as former tutor, his blocking of an audience, and the Báb's confinement at Máh-Kú and Chihríq. Its weaknesses: it quotes no primary source such as Shoghi Effendi or Nabíl, its numbered citations are opaque, and the claim that the Báb offered to heal the Shah is given without a clear source.

verdict.gaps: B gave more context than A: Áqásí's dates, his position as the Shah's tutor and spiritual adviser, the blocked audience in Tehran, the confinement at Máh-Kú and Chihríq, and his fear that the movement could destabilise the state. Neither answer drew on Nabíl's account of Áqásí.

messages.content: Who were the Seven Martyrs of Ṭihrán, and how did each die?

perplexity.text:
The **Seven Martyrs of Ṭihrán** were prominent Bábís publicly executed in Ṭihrán in 1850 after refusing to renounce their faith. They were:

- **Ḥájí Mírzá Siyyid ʿAlí** — a leading merchant of Shíráz and the Báb’s maternal uncle; he was beheaded first.[1][2]
- **Mírzá Qurbán-ʿAlí** — a revered dervish; he was beheaded second.[1][2]
- **Ḥájí Mullá Ismáʿíl-i-Qumí** — a learned religious scholar; he was beheaded.[3]
- **Mullá ʿAbdu’l-Wahháb-i-Qazvíní** — a teacher and scholar of religious law; he was beheaded.[4]
- **Ḥájí Muḥammad-Taqíy-i-Káshání** — a merchant; he was beheaded.[4]
- **Siyyid Murtaḍáy-i-Zanjání** — a merchant from Zanján; he was beheaded.[1]
- **Muḥammad-Ḥusayn-i-Marághihí** — a quiet believer who refused to speak to his captors; he was beheaded.[3]

The executioners killed the first four separately. The final three—**Muḥammad-Taqí, Siyyid Murtaḍá, and Muḥammad-Ḥusayn**—each pleaded to die before the others; their insistence was so strong that they were beheaded simultaneously.[1][4] Thus, although the method was the same for all seven, the accounts especially emphasize their voluntary eagerness and refusal to recant.[2][5]

current.text:
The Seven Martyrs of Ṭihrán were a group of prominent believers executed in February 1850 during the persecution under the Qájár administration. While the texts I can search note their collective tragedy in the Sabzih-Maydán—where their bodies were exposed to indignities—and mention Mírzá ‘Alí-í-Sabzavárí as one of the seven who proclaimed the Cause just before being beheaded, this search does not contain the detailed names and specific death of each individual.

To explore their identities and martyrdoms further, one might examine works detailing early Persian history or seek passages discussing the specific records preserved by Nabíl and Bahá'u'lláh.

current.why: Gives no names and no account of how any of them died. Its one specific claim is wrong: 'Mírzá ʿAlí-i-Sabzavárí' was not one of the Seven. Pointing the reader to Nabíl is fair, but the answer simply admits it has nothing.

perplexity.why: Answers the question the way Nabíl's account does. It names the Báb's maternal uncle and Mírzá Qurbán-ʿAlí as the first two to die, and correctly says the last three were beheaded together because each begged to go first. But it has errors: it puts Mullá ʿAbdu'l-Wahháb-i-Qazvíní on the list instead of Siyyid Ḥusayn-i-Turshízí, the mujtahid, and it calls Ḥájí Muḥammad-Taqí 'Káshání' where Nabíl has 'Kirmání'. It also leaves out well-known details, such as Qurbán-ʿAlí's verse and the botched first blow, and the per-martyr descriptions are thin.

verdict.gaps: Neither answer is clearly marked as Anís. B gave the actual names and the order of execution taken from Nabíl's narrative; A gave none.

messages.content: On what date did the Báb declare His mission — Gregorian and Islamic — and where exactly in Shíráz did it take place?

perplexity.text:
The Báb declared His mission on **23 May 1844**, corresponding to **5 Jumádá al-Awwal 1260 AH** in the Islamic lunar calendar.[1][2]

The declaration took place **shortly after sunset on the evening of 22 May**, in **the Báb’s own house in Shíráz**, during His meeting with Mullá Husayn. The house—now destroyed—was located in the **Old City of Shíráz**, traditionally identified as the **house of the Báb in the Khán neighborhood**, near the **Masjid-i-Ilkhání**.[1][2]

current.text:
The Báb declared His mission on the evening of May 23, 1844 (corresponding to the 5th day of Jamadi'u'l-Awal 1260 A.H., as noted in the editorial apparatus of [*The River of Life*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/bahaullah_the-river-of-life-a-selection-from-the-teachings)), in the upper chamber of a modest residence located in an obscure corner of Shíráz.

The sources for this event span different layers of literature. Revealed Scripture includes the Báb's own writings as presented in [*The Seven Proofs (Dalá'il-i-Sab'ih)*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/the-bab_the-seven-proofs-dalail-i-sabih). Authorized interpretation is provided by Shoghi Effendi in [*God Passes By*](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_26&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_3h.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_3h.683) and through his [*Uncompiled Published Letters*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20897), as well as by ‘Abdu’l-Bahá in [*Divine Philosophy*](https://oceanlibrary.com/divine-philosophy_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_12&selectionString=abdu_l_baha_on_divine_philosophy_bahai_ocean_en-bl32.0~abdu_l_baha_on_divine_philosophy_bahai_ocean_en-bl32.474). Official exposition and compilations, such as [*Bahá’í Sacred Writings*](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-sacred-writings/?paraId=para_1026&selectionString=baha_i_sacred_writings_en-blv1.0~baha_i_sacred_writings_en-blv1.960), also record the date and significance of the event. (Guidance from the Universal House of Justice, by contrast, pertains to administration, laws, and current direction rather than the interpretation of scripture.)

The precise setting and timing of this declaration are described by Shoghi Effendi:

> ["The opening scene of the initial act of this great drama was laid in the upper chamber of the modest residence of the son of a mercer of S̱híráz, in an obscure corner of that city. The time was the hour before sunset, on the 22nd day of May, 1844."]](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_26&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_3h.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_3h.683) [*God Passes By*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21310)

current.why: Gives the correct Islamic date (5 Jamádiyu'l-Avval 1260) and quotes Shoghi Effendi's God Passes By on the upper chamber of the Báb's house in Shíráz, which is the right primary source. But it says 'evening of May 23', which contradicts its own quotation (22 May). It leaves out the exact hour from Nabíl (two hours and eleven minutes after sunset) and pads the answer with irrelevant talk about layers of authority.

perplexity.why: Correctly handles the eve-of-22-May / 23-May framing and the Hijri date. But 'shortly after sunset' is imprecise, since the declaration came two hours and eleven minutes after sunset. The neighbourhood and mosque details ('Khán neighborhood', 'Masjid-i-Ilkhání') look unsupported or invented. It quotes no primary source, and its footnote markers point to no listed references.

verdict.gaps: Neither answer gives Nabíl's precise timing (two hours and eleven minutes after sunset on 22 May), the meeting with Mullá Ḥusayn at the Kázirún gate, or the Báb's own words ('This night, this very hour…'). Neither notes that the house was destroyed in 1979.

Máh-Kú is a town with a mountain fortress located in the northwest corner of Iranian Adharbayjan, near the border with Turkey. messages.content: When and where was the conference of Badasht held, and who provided for it?

perplexity.text:
The Conference of Badasht was held for **22 days, from June 26 to July 17, 1848**, in the village of **Badasht near Shahrud, in present-day Semnan Province, Iran**.[1][2]

It was **organized, hosted, and financed by Bahá’u’lláh**, who rented three gardens for himself, Quddús, and Táhirih and provided hospitality for the 81 attendees.[2][3]

current.text:
The conference of Badasht was held in a hamlet in the northeast of Persia (Khurasán) in June 1848, and the physical arrangements and provisions were supplied entirely by Bahá'u'lláh.

In the authorized interpretation of Shoghi Effendi, 
> ["The scene of such a challenging and far-reaching proclamation was the hamlet of Badas̱ht, where Bahá’u’lláh had rented, amidst pleasant surroundings, three gardens, one of which He assigned to Quddús, another to Ṭáhirih, whilst the third He reserved for Himself. The eighty-one disciples who had gathered from various provinces were His guests from the day of their arrival to the day they dispersed."](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_87&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_56.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_56.798)
> — [*God Passes By*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21310)

perplexity.why: Gets the main facts right: 22 days in summer 1848, near Shahrud, 81 attendees, and Bahá'u'lláh renting three gardens and hosting everyone. But the footnotes [1][2][3] point to no real sources, and the exact dates (June 26 to July 17) are a scholarly reconstruction presented as settled fact. It quotes no primary account.

current.why: Rests the answer on Shoghi Effendi's own account in God Passes By, quoted accurately: the three rented gardens, the 81 guests, and Bahá'u'lláh hosting them throughout. That is the right kind of source for a history question. Weaknesses: calling a historical account an 'authorized interpretation' is a slip; the location is vague, as Badasht lies near Shahrud on the edge of Khurasan; and it gives only 'June 1848', leaving out that the gathering lasted 22 days and ran into July.

verdict.gaps: Answer A gives more precise details: the 22-day length, the nearby town of Shahrud and the modern province (Semnan).

perplexity.text: The siege of Shaykh Ṭabarsí ended in **May 1849**, specifically on **May 10, 1849**.[1][7] The shrine is located in **Mazandaran Province, northern Iran**, about 14 miles southeast of present-day **Babol**.[1][3]

perplexity.text:
The Báb—born **Siyyid ʿAlí-Muḥammad**—was born in **Shiraz, Persia (modern-day Iran), on October 20, 1819** (the first day of Muḥarram 1235 AH).[1][3]

His parents were **Siyyid Muḥammad-Riḍá**, a merchant, and **Fáṭimih-Bágum**. Both were descendants of the Prophet Muhammad.[3][6]

The Báb was born in Shíráz in October 1819, the son of Siyyid Muḥammad-Riḍá, a merchant, and was brought up by His maternal uncle after His father's early death.

As recorded in [*A Traveler’s Narrative*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20899), He "was born in the year one thousand two hundred and thirty-five [A.H.] on the first day of Muḥarram, and when after a few years His father Siyyid Muḥammad-Riḍá died, He was brought up in S̱híráz in the arms of His maternal uncle Mírzá Siyyid ‘Alí the merchant" ([A Traveler’s Narrative](https://oceanlibrary.com/travelers-narrative_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_10&selectionString=abdu-l-baha-traveler-s-narrative-ocean_en_31.0~abdu-l-baha-traveler-s-narrative-ocean_en_31.491)) — *A Traveler’s Narrative*.

But it never names the mother, which the reader asked for, and it gives only 'October 1819' rather than the exact Gregorian date.

messages.content: Give me a timeline of the Báb's life from His birth to His martyrdom, with the places at each stage.

perplexity.text:
- **20 October 1819 — Birth:** The Báb, born Siyyid ʿAlí-Muḥammad, was born in **Shiraz, Persia (present-day Iran)**.[1][3]
- **Childhood and youth — Shiraz:** He was raised in Shiraz in a family of prosperous merchants and later worked in the family’s commercial business.[3]
- **1839–1841 — Bushihr:** He lived and worked as a merchant in **Bushihr**, a Persian Gulf port.[1]
- **1841–1844 — Karbala:** He traveled to **Karbala, Iraq**, where He studied under Siyyid Kázim-i-Rashtí, a prominent religious leader.[3]
- **22–23 May 1844 — Shiraz:** Returning to **Shiraz**, He declared His mission to Mullá Ḥusayn, becoming the Báb and announcing the imminent appearance of “Him Whom God shall make manifest.”[3]
- **1844 — Shiraz and other cities:** He sent His first disciples throughout Persia and Iraq to proclaim His message.[1]
- **September–December 1844 — Bushihr and Mecca:** He departed from **Bushihr** for pilgrimage, traveling by sea to **Mecca**. At the Kaaba, He publicly announced His station and addressed the Sharif of Mecca.[1][3]
- **June 1845 — Shiraz:** He returned to **Shiraz**, where the governor and clergy opposed Him. He was publicly interrogated, placed under restrictions, and later confined.[1]
- **September 1846 — Isfahan:** Expelled from Shiraz, He traveled to **Isfahan**, where Governor Manúchihr Khán protected Him and arranged for Him to reside discreetly.[1][3]
- **1847 — Kashan and Tehran:** After the governor’s death, the Báb was summoned toward **Tehran**. On the journey He passed through **Kashan** and was eventually taken to **Tabriz**.[1][3]
- **July 1847–April 1848 — Máh-Kú:** He was imprisoned in the remote fortress of **Máh-Kú**, near Persia’s northwestern frontier.[3]
- **April 1848–July 1850 — Chihríq:** He was transferred to the fortress of **Chihríq**, where He remained for most of the final two years of His life.[3]
- **July 1848 — Tabriz:** He was taken to **Tabriz**, interrogated before religious and government authorities, and bastinadoed after asserting His prophetic mission.[3][5]
- **1850 — Tabriz:** Returned to Chihríq, He was later brought back to **Tabriz** on the orders of the Grand Vizier.[3][10]
- **9 July 1850 — Martyrdom in Tabriz:** The Báb was executed by firing squad in the barracks square of **Tabriz**, at the age of 30.[2][6][10]

current.text:
The Báb’s earthly life spans from His birth in Shíráz in October 1819 to His public declaration in 1844, followed by a six-year ministry of imprisonment across Persia that ended with His martyrdom in Tabríz in 1850.

As recounted by ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, after proclaiming His mission in Shíráz, the Báb journeyed to Iṣfahán to escape a famine, was arrested and sent to Tabríz, transferred to Máh-Kú, and finally imprisoned in the castle of Chihríq before returning to Tabríz for His execution ([Talk in Cambridge on the declaration of the Báb](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/core-talks/abdul-baha_talk-in-cambridge-on-the-declaration-of-the-bab#p7)). Shoghi Effendi notes that His banishment to the mountains of Áḏhirbáyján included *"His nine months’ unbroken confinement in the fortress of Máh-Kú, and His subsequent incarceration in the fortress of C̱hihríq"* ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_55&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_4a.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_4a.1916)).

*(Note on sources: Revealed Scripture includes the writings of the Báb, such as [The Seven Proofs (Dalá'il-i-Sab'ih)](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/the-bab_the-seven-proofs-dalail-i-sabih#p177). Authorized interpretation is found in the works of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá and Shoghi Effendi. Universal House of Justice guidance pertains to administration and laws rather than doctrine, while history, scholarship, and community practice represent distinct layers of study.)*

perplexity.why: Gives the dated, place-by-place timeline the reader asked for, and most dates are right (birth 1819, Declaration 1844, pilgrimage, Isfahan 1846, Máh-Kú, Chihríq, martyrdom 9 July 1850). But it has real errors. It places Him in Karbala from 1841 to 1844 when His stay was about a year, and says He 'studied under' Siyyid Kázim, which the primary accounts deny. The July 1848 Tabriz trial is listed after the Chihríq period, which muddles the order. It omits Kulayn, the Báb's marriage and the return via Bushihr in 1845, and its footnote numbers point to sources that are never given.

current.why: Rightly draws on primary voices ('Abdu'l-Bahá and God Passes By), but it does not give a timeline. It has almost no dates and leaves out Mecca, Kashan, Kulayn and the 1848 Tabriz trial. Its source note pads the answer without helping the reader.

verdict.gaps: none

messages.content: Lay out the sequence of the three major Bábí upheavals — Ṭabarsí, Nayríz and Zanján — with their dates and leaders.

perplexity.text:
The three major Bábí upheavals occurred in this sequence:

1. **Shaykh Ṭabarsí (Māzandarān): October 1848–9 May 1849**  
   Led principally by **Mullá Ḥusayn-i-Bushrú’í** and **Quddús** (Mullá Muḥammad ʿAlí of Bārfurūsh); the Qajar forces were commanded by **Prince Mihdí-Qulí Mírzá**.[1][7]

2. **Nayríz (Fars): 27 May–21 June 1850**  
   Led by **Siyyid Yaḥyá Dárábí**, known as **Vaḥíd**. This was the first of the two major upheavals in 1850 and ended with the betrayal and massacre of the Bábí defenders.[2][6][9]

3. **Zanjān: May 1850–January 1851**  
   Led by **Ḥujjat**—Mullá Muḥammad-ʿAlí al-Zanjání. Although it began shortly before Nayríz ended, it continued much longer; its commonly given dates are **13 May 1850–January 1851**.[3][6][9]

Thus, the chronological order is **Ṭabarsí → Nayríz → Zanjān**, with **Nayríz and Zanjān overlapping in 1850**.

current.text:
The major Bábí upheavals unfolded across Persia in the early years of the Faith, beginning with Shaykh Ṭabarsí in Máh-Mázindarán, followed by Nayríz in Fárs, and culminating in Zanján. Shoghi Effendi notes that in each of these episodes, Bábís were "driven to desperation, withdrew in concert from their houses to a chosen retreat and, erecting defensive works about them, defied in arms further pursuit" ([Uncompiled Published Letters](https://oceanlibrary.com/uncompiled-published-letters_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_2761&selectionString=published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl2fg.0~published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl2fg.824) - Shoghi Effendi).

The sequence and leadership are detailed in the authorized interpretations and historical records:
- **Shaykh Ṭabarsí (Mázindarán):** Began in the late summer of 1848 and lasted until the spring of 1849, led initially by Mullá Ḥusayn of Buṣhrúyih ([*A Hymn to Love (Sáqí, bi-dih ábí)*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/bahaullah_a-hymn-to-love-saqi-bi-dih-abi)).
- **Nayríz (Fárs):** Occurred in the late spring of 1850 (*A Hymn to Love (Sáqí, bi-dih ábí)*), with Siyyid Yaḥyá of Dáráb serving as the "leader and arbiter" ([A Traveler’s Narrative](https://oceanlibrary.com/travelers-narrative_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_59&selectionString=abdu-l-baha-traveler-s-narrative-ocean_en_4e.0~abdu-l-baha-traveler-s-narrative-ocean_en_4e.795) - ‘Abdu’l-Bahá).
- **Zanján:** Besieged under the military and clerical attack, with Mullá Muḥammad-‘Alí the mujtahid acting as chief ([A Traveler’s Narrative](https://oceanlibrary.com/travelers-narrative_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_59&selectionString=abdu-l-baha-traveler-s-narrative-ocean_en_4e.0~abdu-l-baha-traveler-s-narrative-ocean_en_4e.795) - ‘Abdu’l-Bahá).

current.why: Its strengths are primary sources: Shoghi Effendi's description of how the Bábís withdrew and defended themselves, and 'Abdu'l-Bahá's A Traveller's Narrative for the leaders of Nayríz and Zanján. But it gives no dates for Zanján, leaves out Quddús at Ṭabarsí, and puts the start of Ṭabarsí too early ('late summer 1848'; the siege began in October). It takes its dates from the notes to a tablet translation, an odd and unlabelled source. It also calls historical records 'authorized interpretations', and it never names Ḥujjat or Vaḥíd by their titles.

messages.content: What were the stages of the Báb's journey from Iṣfahán to Máh-Kú — which towns did He pass through and roughly when?

perplexity.text:
The route was not a single uninterrupted march: the escort first took the Báb **north toward Ṭihrán**, then diverted Him west and north-west to **Máh-Kú**.

| Stage | Place | Approximate date |
|---|---|---|
| Departure from Iṣfahán | Iṣfahán | **March 1847**, after the death of Manúchihr Khán |
| First major stop | **Káshán** | About **20–22 March 1847**; He stayed three nights and celebrated Naw-Rúz there[1] |
| En route to Ṭihrán | **Qum** | Late March; the party passed by without entering the city[1] |
| Approach to the capital | **Kinár-Gird** | About **28 March 1847**, roughly 45 km south-east of Ṭihrán[1] |
| Diversion from Ṭihrán | **Kulayn** | Late March–April 1847; the prime minister ordered the escort to stop there instead of entering Ṭihrán[1] |
| Interim northern stage | **Siyáh-Dahán**, near Qazvín | During the ensuing journey north-west; the Báb’s stay in this area is generally placed in **spring–summer 1847**[2] |
| Major city on the final route | **Tabríz** | Probably **June–July 1847**; He remained there about 40 days[3] |
| Destination | **Máh-Kú** | Reached in **late summer 1847**, traditionally dated around **17 July 1847** in one detailed chronology[4] |

In compact form, the itinerary was therefore:

**Iṣfahán → Káshán → Qum (bypassed) → Kinár-Gird → Kulayn → the Qazvín/Siyáh-Dahán area → Tabríz → Máh-Kú.**

The dating is clearest for Káshán, Kinár-Gird, and the general arrival at Máh-Kú; the precise dates of the intermediate north-western stages are less certain. Some accounts summarize the route simply as Iṣfahán–Ṭihrán–Tabríz–Máh-Kú, because Kulayn and the stop near Qazvín were temporary halts rather than principal destinations.[5]

To look closer at the historical record of that route, we might search for specific accounts of His transfer under guard toward the northwest.

messages.content: In what order did the Letters of the Living recognize the Báb, and roughly when did each arrive in Shíráz?

perplexity.text:
The recognition order, with **approximate arrival in Shíráz**, was:

| Order | Letter of the Living | Approximate arrival or recognition |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | **Mullá Ḥusayn-i-Bushrú’í** | Night of the Báb’s declaration, **22–23 May 1844** |
| 2 | **Mullá Muḥammad-Ḥasan Bushrú’í** | Shortly afterward, in **late May or early June** |
| 3 | **Mullá Muḥammad-Báqir Bushrú’í** | With his father and uncle, **late May or early June** |
| 4 | **Mullá ʿAlíy-i-Basṭámí** | Soon after Mullá Ḥusayn, probably **late May or early June** |
| 5 | **Mullá Khudá-Bakhsh-i-Qúchání** | With the same early group, **late May or early June** |
| 6 | **Mullá Ḥasan-i-Bajistání** | With the early group, **late May or early June** |
| 7 | **Siyyid Ḥusayn-i-Yazdí** | With the early group, **late May or early June** |
| 8 | **Mullá Muḥammad-Rawḍih-Khán-i-Yazdí** | With the early group, **late May or early June** |
| 9 | **Saʿíd Hindí** | In the following weeks, probably **June 1844** |
| 10 | **Mullá Maḥmúd-i-Khúʾí** | Probably **June 1844** |
| 11 | **Mullá Jalíl-i-Urúmiyí** | Probably **June 1844** |
| 12 | **Mullá Aḥmad-i-Ibdál-i-Marághí** | Probably **June 1844** |
| 13 | **Mullá Báqir-i-Tabrízí** | Probably **June 1844** |
| 14 | **Mullá Yúsuf-i-Ardibílí** | Probably **June 1844** |
| 15 | **Mullá Muḥammad-ʿAlíy-i-Qazvíní**, later **Quddús’s companion** | Recognition by letter from Ṭáhirih; approximately **June 1844** |
| 16 | **Ṭáhirih** | Recognized the Báb remotely through a letter; **she never went to Shíráz** |

Mullá ʿAlíy-i-Basṭámí recognized the Báb before the other members of his traveling party, but the party’s members were later assigned the formal numerical order as Letters. A later group of roughly thirteen disciples reached Shíráz together in **late June 1844**, while Quddús came last and was recognized as the eighteenth and final Letter.[1][2][3][4]

Ṭáhirih is the exception: she was the only Letter who did not arrive in Shíráz; her recognition and appointment occurred through correspondence, conveyed by her brother-in-law Mullá Muḥammad-ʿAlíy-i-Qazvíní.[2][3]

messages.content: What happened, in order, between the Báb's martyrdom in July 1850 and the attempt on the Sháh's life in August 1852?

perplexity.text:
In chronological order:

1. **July 9, 1850 — The Báb was executed in Tabriz.** His companion, Anís, was also killed, and their bodies were cast outside the city.[1][8]

2. **Late 1850–1851 — The Bábí community was left leaderless and subjected to continuing persecution.** Many prominent Bábís had already been killed or imprisoned, and the movement increasingly operated underground.[2][7]

3. **During this period — Some Bábís came to regard the Sháh as responsible for the Báb’s death and the persecution of his followers.** Two young Bábís, Ṣádiq-i-Tabrízí and Fath’u’lláh-i-Qumí, eventually resolved to avenge these deaths.[9]

4. **August 15, 1852 — The attempt on the Sháh’s life took place near Niávárán, outside Tehran.** The two approached Nāṣiri’d-Dín Shāh as he was setting out and fired at him with a pistol loaded with birdshot. He suffered no serious injury, and the attackers were immediately seized.[1][2][9]

5. **Afterward — The failed attempt triggered a far wider persecution of the Bábís**, including mass arrests and executions and Bahá’u’lláh’s imprisonment in Tehran’s Siyāh-Chāl.[2][4]
